title: Best Age For Business School
summary: An early two-host episode opening with weekly highs and lows (rest when sick, a first AI panel, post-MBA loneliness in a new city) before tackling how old is too old or too young for business school. The hosts, fresh from Stanford GSB and seven years out of HBS, cover average enrollment ages, 2+2 deferred programs and why younger students can get written off, how mid-to-late-30s students with families experience school differently, and Stanford's MSx, executive and distinguished-fellow alternatives.

ideas.idea: When you are sick, resting is your number one job and action item, not a guilty lapse in productivity.
ideas.detail: Jean pushed through illness on adrenaline out of what Cherie calls a trauma response from finance; once she turned off she realized she was sicker than she thought and recovered properly.

ideas.idea: Unlimited PTO in tech is a psychological trick: people take fewer days off than in traditional industries with a mandated 10 days or two weeks.
ideas.detail: Without carefully monitoring their days, tech workers end up working more under discretionary time-off policies.

ideas.idea: Speaking on a panel forces you to formulate opinions in real time, and speaking for yourself is a different, more nervous experience than representing a company.
ideas.detail: Jean did her first public speaking since the pandemic on an XPRIZE AI panel about empathic, humanist AI; she had previously spoken in Vegas, Shanghai, Tel Aviv and Toronto on behalf of Snapchat.

ideas.idea: Small women's gatherings where each person says what they are working on and how others can help are unusually warm, grounded and energizing forms of networking.
ideas.detail: A 25-woman breakfast in Malibu across industries left Jean feeling uplifted and hopeful about what women can do.

ideas.idea: Working for yourself without a boss or program sharply limits incidental human interaction, so you have to manufacture it through alumni events and weekend plans.
ideas.detail: Cherie, approaching 29 and newly in LA with no roots, feels a profound loneliness after leaving the density of business school; New York or SF would have offered friends every night of the week.

ideas.idea: Framing a hard period as temporary lets you sit more comfortably in the discomfort and focus on what the time is good for, like working on yourself.
ideas.detail: Jean applies Sheryl Sandberg's three P's, it's not personal, not pervasive, not permanent, to Cherie's post-MBA transition.

ideas.idea: Pouring time and emotional bandwidth into ushering best friends into marriage while you are in an in-between period creates a dissonance worth noticing, so take some time for yourself.
ideas.detail: Cherie is bridesmaid for two best friends getting married while she is still figuring out her own new chapter.

ideas.idea: The average business school student enrolls at 27 to 29, typically four to five years out of undergrad.
ideas.detail: Jean entered HBS at 26 turning 27 and Cherie entered Stanford GSB at 27 turning 28, both exactly five years after college.

ideas.idea: Apply to business school when your learning curve has flattened and you want a more diverse set of experiences.
ideas.detail: After four and a half years in product management at LinkedIn, Jean told her boss she would either join a startup or go to business school; her VP had gone to GSB and a director to HBS, so it was culturally normal, and prep like the GRE took three and a half years in the background.

ideas.idea: Deferred 2+2 programs admit you in undergrad and hold the seat while you work at least two years, and you can often defer even longer.
ideas.detail: The HBS 2+2 admission rate is reportedly lower than the regular rate, so the committee is betting on potential rather than a work track record.

ideas.idea: Arriving at 24 with only two years of experience can be isolating: in case-method classrooms the richness of discussion comes from work stories, and classmates may condescend to or write off 'the baby of the class'.
ideas.detail: People come to business school to learn from peers and quietly dismiss those they think have nothing to offer; the flip side is the youngest have the most to gain from everyone else.

ideas.idea: If you get into a 2+2 program, take three or more years in the workforce before enrolling so learning is experiential rather than purely academic.
ideas.detail: The hosts' direct advice given the experience gap between 24 and 29 year olds.

ideas.idea: Going to business school in your mid-to-late 30s can be great if it is the right path, but you must tolerate the antics of 20-somethings for whom it is a two-year vacation.
ideas.detail: The oldest classmates were about 36 to 38; some rolled their eyes at Thursday-night party buses to San Francisco, and many came with partners and children, which by definition creates a different experience.

ideas.idea: Stanford's one-year MSx program serves people about ten years into their careers, and there is a real if unspoken tension between MSx and MBA students.
ideas.detail: MSx students (about 90 vs 420 MBAs) see MBAs as lazy vacationers, MBAs see MSx students as grade-focused try-hards, which clashes in shared group projects.

ideas.idea: Executive MBA programs, often company-sponsored and about a week long, are reportedly how HBS makes the majority of its revenue, essentially a B2B business.
ideas.detail: Stanford also has a Distinguished Careers fellowship where people in their 60s apply, are vetted on their careers, and sit ungraded in classes like real estate and private equity.

ideas.idea: Whatever the age gap in a classroom, be kind and say hi; engaging warmly with strangers is a skill and a habit.
ideas.detail: Cherie chats with cashiers and Uber drivers while Jean tends to dissociate; Jean says it is something she admires about her sister.
